content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued updated recommendations on the use of tocolytic therapy to improve outcomes for preterm births. Preterm birth complications are the leading cause of neonatal deaths and deaths in children under five years of age. Babies born prematurely are at higher risk of severe illnesses during childhood, including respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular hemorrhage, necrotizing enterocolitis, and sepsis, as well as long-term complications such as chronic lung disease and neurological disabilities. Addressing preterm birth is critical to reducing neonatal and child mortality globally. In 2021, WHO prioritized updating its recommendations on tocolytic therapy due to new evidence on its efficacy. Tocolytic drugs, which inhibit uterine contractions, can delay preterm labor, allowing time for fetal maturation, administration of antenatal corticosteroids to improve lung development, and in-utero transfer of the mother to a facility equipped to manage preterm infants. The updated recommendation now supports the use of nifedipine for acute and maintenance tocolytic therapy in women at high risk of preterm birth, provided specific conditions are met. The conditions for using nifedipine include: 1. Suspected or diagnosed spontaneous preterm labor. 2. Accurate gestational age assessment between 24 weeks 0 days and 33 weeks 6 days. 3. No contraindications to tocolysis, such as vaginal bleeding, placental abruption, or intrauterine infection. 4. The ability to administer a single course of antenatal corticosteroids and/or transfer the mother to a facility capable of providing adequate care for the preterm infant, including resuscitation, kangaroo mother care, thermal care, feeding support, infection treatment, and respiratory support. 5. Availability of adequate birth care, including the capacity to recognize and manage preterm labor and birth safely. 6. Provision of sufficient information to women and families about the benefits and risks of tocolysis, including the lack of data on long-term outcomes. The updated recommendation supersedes the 2015 WHO guideline, which did not recommend tocolytic therapy due to insufficient evidence of its benefits. The new evidence indicates that nifedipine can improve neonatal outcomes when used appropriately. The primary audience for this recommendation includes healthcare professionals responsible for developing national and local healthcare protocols, maternal and child health program managers, and policymakers. It is also relevant for obstetricians, pediatricians, midwives, nurses, and general practitioners directly involved in the care of pregnant women and preterm infants. Additionally, the recommendation aims to guide the development of training tools and job aids to enhance the delivery of maternal and neonatal care related to preterm birth. The recommendation was developed using WHO’s standardized guideline development procedures, which included identifying priority questions, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, assessing the quality of evidence using the GRADE methodology, and formulating recommendations through an international panel of experts. In summary, WHO now recommends nifedipine as a tocolytic agent for improving preterm birth outcomes under specific conditions. This updated guidance reflects the latest evidence and aims to improve the quality of care and outcomes for women at risk of preterm birth and their infants.
